title: Ravana and Maricha's warning
hook: flatterers are everywhere, says an old rakshasa to his king; the person who tells you the hard truth is rare
carry: pleasant things are easy to find
tomorrow: Ravana and Maricha's warning, part three

segments.voice: Yesterday: Maricha talked Ravana out of the plan, until Shurpanakha shamed him in his court. Pride stung in public is harder to talk down.

Ravana sets out again in his flying chariot, along the coast. Valmiki slows down to paint it: shores lined with coconut palms and sandalwood, pearls drying on the beaches, hermitages of sages, and merchants' ships. Then the chariot lands at Maricha's hermitage a second time. The old rakshasa, in bark clothes and matted hair, welcomes his king with food and water, and asks, carefully: why have you come back?
screen: `A FLYING CHARIOT ALONG THE COAST.` → `PEARLS ON THE BEACHES.` → `WHY HAVE YOU COME BACK?`

segments.voice: Ravana spells out the plan. Turn yourself into a golden deer, spotted with silver, and wander near Rama's hut. Sita will want you. Rama and Lakshmana will go after you. Then I'll take her. Maricha begins with a saying: people who say pleasant things are always easy to find, king. But someone who says what is unpleasant and good for you, and someone who will listen to it, those are rare. Then he tells Ravana the truth he doesn't want. You don't know who Rama is. He wasn't sent to the forest for any crime; he went to keep his father's word. And then a short line in Sanskrit: ramo vigrahavan dharmah. Rama is dharma in bodily form: right living, duty and truth, with a body and a bow. To steal his wife is to walk into a fire. You'll ruin yourself, your city and your people. Look at who's speaking. Not a sage, not a god, not one of Rama's friends, but a rakshasa, Rama's old enemy, once hurled across the sea by him. He has met Rama as an enemy, and that gives his words their weight. He's using everything he knows to save his own king from himself.
screen: `BECOME A GOLDEN DEER.` · `PLEASANT WORDS ARE EASY TO FIND.` · `RAMA IS DHARMA IN BODILY FORM.` · `THE WARNING FROM AN OLD ENEMY.` · then, large: `TRYING TO SAVE HIS KING.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who told you something you didn't want to hear that turned out to be true, and picture their face as they said it. Notice what it cost them, and let a little gratitude rise. If a hard truth you've meant to say kindly to someone comes to mind, just hold it too, without planning.
Dharma, right living, duty, truth: Maricha tells Ravana that flatterers are easy to find, but Rama is dharma in bodily form.
Your line: pleasant things are easy to find. The rare friend says the hard thing, and the rare listener hears it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Maricha's line ramo vigrahavan dharmah, Rama is dharma in bodily form, is quoted on its own in Hindu teaching, as are his lines on rare, honest advice.

fork.setup: you're Maricha. your king wants you to lure Rama away so he can steal Sita. what do you tell him?
options: the hard truth: Rama is dharma itself, and this will ruin you.
fork.reveal: Maricha tells him the hard truth, plainly. tomorrow: what Ravana does with it.

original.note: Sanskrit: 'Rama is dharma with a body,' Maricha's line in Aranya 37.

trapdoor: what you thought: Maricha is just Ravana's helper.
what it means: he's the one who warns Ravana, and calls Rama dharma itself.
what a scholar hears: Aranya 37 holds both the verse on rare honest advice and 'ramo vigrahavan dharmah', two lines that stand on their own as sayings.

chat.says: What did Maricha mean when he called Rama dharma in bodily form?
options: That Rama is right living, duty and truth in a person, so attacking him is walking into fire.
That Rama was sent to the forest as a punishment, so he knew the law better than anyone.
That Rama was a strict judge who would hunt down and punish every rakshasa in the forest.
chat.meaning: Maricha says Rama went to the forest to keep his father's word: dharma with a body and a bow. Stealing his wife would bring ruin.

ramo vigrahavan dharmah.meaning: Sanskrit: Rama is dharma in bodily form

Maricha.meaning: the old rakshasa who warns his king

rakshasa.meaning: a demon-like being of the forest and of Lanka

recall: a companion on the path of dharma
